risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 is the right instrument and low confidence follows from one critical item not met (11). I agree with item 11: the authors judge every comparison intransitive (3.9) yet chain the trials without justification, and the dropout heterogeneity (I² 72.5%) is not investigated. The rating concerns the network estimates; the trial inventory remains citable as such.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor agreed, as the abstract's conclusion carries the low-quality caveat. Two further widenings: the 1st discussion paragraph (p. 6) calls olanzapine and quetiapine 'probably superior' to aripiprazole and risperidone, stronger than the abstract's 'may be a preferred'; and the abstract's results sentence states that both 'were superior' to risperidone without saying that the estimates are indirect only.

missed: One degree of freedom for heterogeneity (editors' reasoning from Table 1 and Fig. 2): six two-arm trials and six drugs leave 6 − 5 = 1 degree of freedom, all of it from the two aripiprazole–risperidone trials (Farnia 2014; Wang 2016), since the network has no closed loop. The global I² values (0% for main symptoms, 72.5% for dropout; 3.7, Fig. 3 legend) therefore describe only that pair, and the authors' decision not to downgrade main symptoms and dropout for inconsistency (3.9, I² below 75%) says nothing about agreement across the network. A claim should not cite the 0% as evidence of consistency.

Shared investigators: the two Chinese trials (Wang 2016 and Wang 2020) share G. Wang, W. Hao and M. C. Chawarski (reference list, p. 8), so they are not independent teams; this bears on any replication count.

Main and positive outcomes overlap: in two of the four positive-symptom trials (Farnia, Samiei) the main-symptom scale is itself the SAPS (Table 1), and the haloperidol–risperidone estimate is identical in both networks (−0.60, −1.20 to 0.01; Fig. 3A and 3B). The positive-symptom result is not independent confirmation of the main-symptom result.

A seventh head-to-head trial outside the review's definition: the excluded olanzapine–haloperidol trial in mental disorders due to amphetamine-type stimulants (Xue 2018) also found no difference (discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 6).
